title: Freedom Is Understanding and Complying with Necessity
author: Mingde
excerpt: Freedom is the understanding of and compliance with necessity — inserting what has no thickness into what has space. Zhuangzi said: “Insert what has no thickness into what has space, and how ample is the room — there is sure to be more than enough for the blade to move.” (Translation: to run the thinnest of blades through the spaces between sinew and bone — how broad, how full of room it is! — from Zhuangzi · The Mastery of Nurturing Life)

inline.s: Appendix: Cook Ding Carves the Ox
Freedom is the understanding of and compliance with necessity — inserting what has no thickness into what has space. Zhuangzi said:
“Insert what has no thickness into what has space, and how ample is the room — there is sure to be more than enough for the blade to move.”
(Translation: to run the thinnest of blades through the spaces between sinew and bone — how broad, how full of room it is! — from Zhuangzi
The Mastery of Nurturing Life)

Because Cook Ding had mastered the structure and workings of the ox’s body (understanding necessity), he ran his knife through the spaces (complying with necessity), and therefore found it broad and full of room (freedom).
Question: Does life, then, not require effort and achievement?
Answer: It does. In fact, understanding and complying with necessity is the mastery and application of objective law. Only in this way can one
bring subjective initiative to its utmost
, as Cook Ding did in carving the ox. For a Buddhist practitioner, however,
what is needed is
true effort and true achievement

— ending birth and death and escaping the cycle of rebirth; this alone is what a true hero does! All the rest is empty: the struggle for fame and gain, wealth and honor, success and renown — all no more than a dream of millet. As it is said, “Each passing thing is judged as fair or foul,
but in the end, not one of them concerns us at all

.” Moreover, to end birth and death, what is sought depends on oneself, and the mastery lies wholly in one’s own hands; but fame, wealth, and honor depend on others and can be achieved only when conditions converge. Therefore the great majority of people, even plotting every scheme and staking their very lives, may never reach the step of “wealth, honor, success, and renown” — and how can one count the pain, defeat, remorse, and torment in between, along with the karmic debts incurred? The Dream of the Red Chamber
Song of the Good and the Bad says:

“All day they grieve they have gathered not enough; when much is gathered, their eyes have closed for good.” “Where are the generals and statesmen of old and new today? A mound of weeds upon a desolate grave — that is all.”
Yang Sheng’an’s Riverside Fairy says:
“Right and wrong, success and ruin, turn to naught in the turn of a head; the green hills still stand as of old; how many times has the setting sun glowed red!”
Wang Rixiu’s Longshu’s Expanded Pure Land Writings says:
“When impermanence arrives one day, you know you were a person in a dream; of the ten thousand things none can you carry away — only karma follows you.”

[This alone is what a true hero does] The Commentary on Master Hanshan’s Chronicle records: At the age of ten, with my mother urging my studies very strictly, I (as Master Hanshan calls himself) found it very hard. So I asked my mother: “What is studying for?” Mother said: “To become an official.” I asked: “What kind of official?” Mother said: “Start small, and if you are capable you can rise to be prime minister.” I asked: “And after becoming prime minister?” Mother said: “Then you step down (through age, illness, death, or demotion).” I said: “What a pity to toil a whole life only to step down at the end — what use is it? I only want to do something that never steps down.” Mother said: “A good-for-nothing like you can only be a wandering monk.” I asked: “What is a wandering monk, and what good is it?” Mother said: “A monk is a disciple of the Buddha, who travels everywhere under heaven, free and at ease, with offerings wherever he goes.” I said: “That would suit me perfectly.” Mother said: “I only fear you have not the good fortune for it!” I asked: “Why should I need good fortune?” Mother said: “In the world, first-place scholars are common, but to leave home and become a Buddha — where is that common?” I said: “I have this fortune; I only fear that Mother cannot bear to let me go.” Mother said: “If you have this fortune, I can bear to let you go.” And so I silently kept these words in my heart. (For the original text, see
the Commentary on Master Hanshan’s Chronicle
) [Wandering monk] A monk who travels to all quarters, also called a mendicant monk. A verse says:
“One bowl, a thousand households’ rice; alone I wander ten thousand li
(for the great matter of ending birth and death)
; I beg my way through spring and autumn
(begging for food and delivering beings, year after year)
Question: Does complying with necessity mean submitting to the arrangements of fate?

Answer: It does not mean submitting to the arrangements of fate, but wisely reshaping one’s fate. Mr. Liaofan and Mr. Yu Jingyi both reshaped their own fates through understanding and complying with necessity, and thus achieved brilliant results; for details see
the Commentary on Liaofan’s Four Lessons
and
the Commentary on the Record of Yu Jingyi’s Encounter with the Kitchen God

. Of the many, many people who wished to reshape their fates but did not succeed, some understood necessity insufficiently, some understood it wrongly, and some, though they understood it correctly, lacked the power of execution to comply.
Question: Does complying with necessity mean drifting with the current?
Answer: Complying with necessity is to avoid needless obstacles and dangers (there is no point in hacking at bone with the blade when there is space in plenty),
so as to fulfill the mission of this present life
(anything at all is utterly insignificant beside the mission of this life), rather than drifting and sinking aimlessly in the sea of birth and death.
In fact, complying with necessity is the respect for, obedience to, and
application

of objective law. People often say: “You have the freedom to jump from a building, and you have the freedom to break your legs.” This describes those who, with stairs available, willfully insist on jumping.
Cook Ding Carves the Ox” is taken from the Zhuangzi

The Mastery of Nurturing Life. This is the third chapter of the whole Zhuangzi, belonging to the Inner Chapters, and it discusses the way of nurturing life. The “nurturing life” spoken of here is not nurture in the modern sense, but preserving the body (keeping oneself whole), fulfilling life (keeping one’s nature whole), nourishing the new (tending the fresh impulse of life), and completing one’s years (living out one’s natural span).
[Nourishing the new] Tending the fresh impulse of life. “Qin” (new) is interchangeable with “xin” (new), meaning renewal. For example: “The new ministers advance while the old retreat.” (Han Feizi
Signs of Ruin)
“Cook
páo
Ding was carving an ox for King Wen Hui. Wherever his hand touched, his shoulder leaned, his foot stepped, his knee pressed
yǐ
, with a hiss
huā
and a thud, and a swish as his knife slid through
huō
, every sound was in tune
zhòng
, keeping time with the Dance of the Mulberry Grove, and matching
zhòng
the melody of the Jingshou music.”

Cook Ding was slaughtering an ox for King Wen Hui. The touch of his hands, the press of his shoulders, the tread of his feet, the brace of his knees, the sound of skin and flesh parting, the swish of the knife advancing — all were musical sounds (not noise), keeping to the rhythm of the Mulberry Grove dance and the melody of the Jingshou music.
[Cook (
páo
) Ding] A cook. [To brace (
yǐ
)] To press and hold with the knee. [With a hiss (
huā
)] The sounds of skin and flesh parting, echoing one another.
[Swish (
huō
)] An onomatopoeia for various sounds.
[To advance the knife] To move the knife forward. [In tune (
zhòng
)] In accord with the rhythm and melody of music.
[The melody of Jingshou] Jingshou was, by legend, the name of a piece of music from the time of Emperor Yao; hui means melody.
“King Wen Hui said: ‘Wonderful! How has your skill reached such a height!’”
King Wen Hui said: Wonderful! That the skill of carving an ox could reach such a height!
“Cook Ding put down his knife and replied: ‘What I love
hào
is the Way, which advances beyond skill. When I first began carving oxen, I saw nothing but whole oxen. After three years, I no longer saw a whole ox.’”

Cook Ding put down his butcher’s knife and said: What I love is the Way, which has already gone beyond the scope of mere skill. When I first began carving oxen, all I saw were whole oxen. After three years, I no longer saw a whole ox, but only the spaces where the knife might move.
[The Way] The laws of things.
[Advances beyond skill] Goes beyond the scope of skill. Here “advances” means to surpass.
“At present, I meet it with the spirit and do not look with the eyes; the senses’ knowing stops and the spirit’s wish proceeds. Following the natural grain, I pierce the great clefts
xì
, interchangeable with “gap”)
, guide the knife through the great hollows
kuǎn
, hollow places)
, and go by what is inherently so. The places where the sinews
zhī
, interchangeable with “branch”)
and vessels join the bones
qǐ
, where flesh and bone are tightly joined)
I have never touched, much less the great bones
gū
, the big bones)

By now, I no longer look with my eyes at all, but meet it with the spirit; my vision stops while the spirit moves. Following the ox’s inherent structure, I insert the sharp blade into the great clefts where sinew joins bone, then guide it along the hollows between the joints. Because I run the knife entirely according to the ox’s inherent structure, I never even touch the places where vessels and sinews interconnect and bone and flesh interlace, let alone those great bones!
[Organ (guan)] An organ, here the eye. [Natural grain] Here the inherent structure of the ox’s body. [Pierce the great clefts (
xì
)] Pi, to thrust in; xi, interchangeable with “gap,” here the spaces between sinew, tendon, and bone. [Guide through the great hollows (
kuǎn
)] To travel along the hollows between the joints. Dao, the same as “guide,” to follow; kuan (
kuǎn
), a hollow place, here the larger hollows between the joints. [Sinews and vessels joining the bones] Ji (
zhī
), interchangeable with “branch,” referring to the branch vessels; jing, the channels. “Ji jing” refers to the places where the channels gather. Ken, the flesh attached to the bone; qing (
qǐ
), the places where flesh and bone are tightly joined. [Gu (
gū
)] The big bones.

“A good cook changes his knife once a year, because he cuts; an ordinary cook changes his knife every month, because he hacks. My knife has now been in use for nineteen years and has carved several thousand oxen, yet the blade is as if freshly sharpened. There are spaces between the joints, and the blade has no thickness. Inserting what has no thickness into what has space, there is ample room — more than enough for the blade to move freely! That is why, after nineteen years, the blade is still as if freshly sharpened.”

A good cook changes his knife once a year because he cuts; an ordinary cook changes his knife every month because he hacks. This knife of mine has been in use for nineteen years and has carved several thousand oxen, yet the blade is still as sharp as when it was first whetted. Because between the joints and between the sinews there is always space, while the blade is extremely thin. To run the thinnest of blades through these spaces — how broad, how full of room it is! That is why, after nineteen years of use, the blade is still as sharp as when it was first whetted.

[Ordinary cook] An average cook. Zu means the multitude. [To hack] To cut with force. [Freshly sharpened] Just whetted on the grindstone. Fa means to bring out the edge, to whet or sharpen a knife or ax; xing (
xíng
) is the grindstone. [Ample] Broad.

“Nevertheless, whenever I come to a place where the joints are knotted, I see that it is difficult, and I grow wary and alert; my gaze comes to rest, my movements grow slow, and I move the knife ever so slightly. Then with a crack the ox is already parted, like a clod of earth collapsing to the ground.”

Even so, whenever I come to a place where sinew and bone are knotted together, I know it is a difficult pass, and I become extremely careful and cautious; my gaze fixes, my movements slow, and I run the knife lightly. Once the difficult pass is crossed, the whole ox falls apart with a crack, like earth piled upon the ground.
[Whenever I come to a knot] Whenever I come to a place where sinew and bone are knotted together. Zu means the places where bone joints and sinews gather and interlace. [Wary (
chù
)] The manner of being careful and cautious.
[Parted with a crack] The whole ox falls apart with a crack. Huo (
huò
) is the sound of the body coming apart.
“I stand with knife in hand, look all around me, and feel utterly satisfied and at ease; then I wipe the knife clean and put it away.”
So I stand with knife in hand, look around on all sides, and feel satisfied and proud of this extraordinary feat; then I wipe the knife clean and put it away.

[Satisfied and at ease] Describes being very pleased with the achievement one has made. Chouchu means the manner of being composed and self-content; man means satisfied; zhi means one’s aspiration. [Like a clod of earth] Like earth piled upon the ground. Wei means to pile up.
[Wipe the knife] To wipe the knife clean. Shan means to wipe.
“King Wen Hui said: ‘Wonderful! Hearing Cook Ding’s words, I have learned how to nurture life.’”
King Wen Hui said: Wonderful! Hearing Cook Ding’s words, I have grasped the principle of nurturing life.
[Learned how to nurture life] The “nurturing life” spoken of in this chapter

is not nurture in the modern sense, but preserving the body (keeping oneself whole), fulfilling life (keeping one’s nature whole), nourishing the new (tending the fresh impulse of life), and completing one’s years (living out one’s natural span). [Nourishing the new] Tending the fresh impulse of life. “Qin” (new) is interchangeable with “xin” (new), meaning renewal. For example: “The new ministers advance while the old retreat.” (Han Feizi · Signs of Ruin)
